title: Part Two, Chapter 3: The Maiden Xquic

verses.t: Here is told of a maiden, the daughter of a lord who is called Cuchumaquic.

Now a maiden, the daughter of a lord who was called Cuchumaquic, and she herself Xquic ("blood"), heard her father's talk of how that tree had borne fruit; and marvelling at what she heard, she said, "Why should I not go and see this tree they talk about? For truly what they say and I hear is very sweet and pleasant." And then she went by herself, and came beneath the tree, which stood opposite the place where the ashes were thrown; and marvelling, she said, "What lovely fruit, and how beautifully this tree bears! I shall not die or perish if I pick one of these fruits." And then the skull that was in the forks of the tree spoke, and said, "What is it that you want? That round thing in the branches of the tree is only bone. Do you perhaps want this?" it said to the maiden. "I want it," said the maiden. "Very well; then stretch out your right hand," said the skull. "Good," said the maiden, and she stretched her right hand up before the skull. And then the skull let fly a spurt of spittle, which came straight into the maiden's hand; and at once, in great haste, she looked at the palm of her hand, and the skull's spittle was no longer in her hand. "I have given you a sign," said the skull, "in my spittle and my saliva. This head of mine will no longer answer, because it is only bone and has no flesh any more. And so it is with the head of any lord: it is adorned only by the flesh, and when he dies, men are frightened of the skull. And so his children are like his spittle and his saliva: if they are the children of a wise and understanding lord, the being of a wise and understanding lord is not lost or put out, but is inherited by his sons and daughters when he begets them. And so I have done with you. And so go up there to the earth, for you shall not die. Hold to the word, for it shall be done." This is what the head of Hun-hun-ahpu and Vucub-hun-ahpu said; and this was the wisdom and command of Huracán, Chipa-caculha and Raxa-caculha; by their command they did it. And so the maiden returned to her house, after many things and commands had been told her. And then she conceived, and sons were conceived in her womb from what was only spittle; and those who were begotten were Hun-hun-ahpu and Xbalanque. And when the maiden had returned to her house and six months had passed, her father Cuchumaquic noticed it.

And as soon as the maiden's pregnancy was noticed by her father, and that she was with child, the lords Hun-came and Vucub-came met in council with Cuchumaquic, and he said, "This daughter of mine is pregnant, lords, and it has come from her wantonness and fornication." This is what Cuchumaquic said when he appeared before the lords. "Very well," they said. "Press her to confess, and we shall see what she says; and let her be taken far away and killed." "Very well, lords," he said. And then he asked his daughter, "Whose is the child you carry in your belly?" And she said, "I have no child, lord father; I have not yet known a man." "Very well," he said, "you are a fornicator. Come, go, you chief lords, go and sacrifice her, and bring her heart in a gourd bowl." This was ordered of the owls, who were four. And then they went and took a gourd bowl, and they went off carrying her; and they also carried a sharp knife to cut her open. And then she said to them, "Do not kill me, messengers, for I am no fornicator; what I carry in my belly was simply begotten. What happened was that I went to amuse myself and see that wonder, the head of Hun-hun-ahpu that is in the place of ashes. So do not kill me, messengers." And they answered, "Then what are we to carry in this gourd in place of your heart? Did the lords not order us to bring them your heart in this gourd? Did they not order us so? We would gladly save you." "Very well," she said. "This heart does not belong to them. And your lot shall not be here; rather you shall have power over men, that they die; and truly that shall be your being, to be deceivers. And Hun-came and Vucub-came shall then be mine; only blood and skulls shall be theirs; that alone shall be theirs, before them. This heart shall not be burned before them. Put the fruit of this tree in the gourd," said the maiden; and the sap of that tree was red. And when the sap came out, they caught it in the gourd, and at once it congealed and became round, and it was put in place of the heart; and its sap was like blood, which she put in place of blood. And then they took out that blood from the sap of the tree, and it was made like blood, and it was very red after it was taken out, on the ground. And then that tree shone because of the maiden; and this tree is called the red dragon's-blood tree, and it was called blood, and because of her it was called blood. "There on the earth you shall have what is yours, and you shall be well rewarded," the maiden said to the owls. "Very well, maiden," they said. "We shall go and take this; and you, go on your way, for we are going to give the lords this exchange for your heart," said the owls. And then they came into the presence of the lords, who were all waiting. "Has it been done?" said Hun-came and Vucub-came. "It is done, lords," they said. "Here is her heart at the bottom of this gourd." "Very well, let us see," said Hun-came and Vucub-came. And taking it up with three fingers, he lifted it up; the blood dripped, and it was very red with blood. "Stir up the fire well and set it on the fire," said Hun-came. And as soon as they dried it over the fire, those of the underworld smelled the fragrance, and they all stood up and were as if entranced over it; truly what they smelled from the smoke of the blood was very sweet. And then, while they were in amazement, the owl and the others who had taken the maiden went away. And so the lords of the underworld were defeated by the maiden; with that semblance they were all deceived.
